prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level and made them a probe of many-body physics, relativity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B043 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, the case that persuades me most is not the headline accuracy but the chain of evidence behind it. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil effects while cancelling the light shift, which allows an ensemble to be interrogated with the statistics of many atoms. The Boulder work then showed that this can be pushed to 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and that interactions in a degenerate fermion gas are something to be controlled and understood. Independent clocks in Sr, Yb and Hg, with direct comparisons between laboratories, show that the result is reproduced and not one group's claim. The consequences are already realised and not promised: gravitational redshift resolved over centimetre scales, constraints on drifts of fundamental constants, and a many-body clock platform. I accept Lindroth's point that the citation should name these physics results and not lean only on metrology. The two-name attribution maps onto the concept and the demonstrated performance, and it is the cleanest on the shortlist. It is distinct in kind from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize, which did not credit the idea of an ensemble in a magic-wavelength lattice.
statement.case_against: The main weakness remains category. Mehlig, Johansson and Olsson read the clock as an extraordinary refinement of a tradition already honoured twice, and no deviation from existing theory has yet been seen. Other lattice-clock groups in Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere contributed, so two names leave out real contributors and the pending redefinition of the second has not happened. Standing alone, a one-part prize also asks more of a single achievement than a two-part prize would. I weigh these seriously, but I do not find that any of them reduces the confirmed science.

responses.point: Pearce, with Danielsson, proposes pairing B043 with IceCube (B010) credited to Halzen alone, so that a measurement achievement sits beside an observational discovery within three names.
responses.response: I considered the pairing and I do not support it. The science of IceCube is not in question, since the diffuse flux is a real discovery. My objection is the credit. A one-name award for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES as precursors and Karle's detector and analysis leadership not clearly separable from Halzen's, would look arbitrary to the community, and neither of you has identified a decisive individual contribution that settles it. Danielsson says he would rather drop that half than invent a trio. I would go further: a prize should not be assembled in order to make the clock look less like measurement. I am content that the clock is sufficient alone, and I keep B010 as an alternative for a year with a cleaner credit.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what physics a clock prize teaches that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not, and notes that no deviation from existing theory has been seen.
responses.response: That is the right test and I have tried to answer it concretely. The 2005 prize gave a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped quantum systems. Neither showed how to hold an ensemble of neutral atoms without perturbing the transition, so a many-atom statistical advantage was not available. The lattice clock also taught something new, namely that interactions and dense spin-polarised fermions are a controllable ingredient and not a limit. I agree that a null result in tests of constants is not evidence of new physics. I still count it as physics, because it tightens constraints, and the geodesy result is a direct observation of gravitational redshift at a scale never reached before. In my first-round reply I put the clock close behind a concept with wide downstream influence, but on reflection I do not think B008 is clearly ahead, given the 2016 overlap you and Olsson raised and the unresolved Mele, Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question.

responses.point: Lindroth said the citation should state the many-body clock results and relativity tests as physics results, not rely only on metrology, and that the Boulder demonstrations of systematic control turned Katori's concept into a standard.
responses.response: I accept both points and I have changed the citation to say so. The concept alone is not the prize, and it was the Boulder control of systematics and the many-body understanding that made the clock a probe of physics. That is also my reply to the discovery-versus-refinement objection. I still resist adding more names. The lattice scheme belongs to Katori, and the demonstrated accuracy and interaction physics belong to Ye. Widening to Lemonde, Pfau, Braunschweig or others would require a larger cap than we have and would blur the distinction from 2005.

responses.point: Olsson prefers twisted bilayer graphene (B029), as a discovery that opened a new regime, and accepts that the maturity gap is the real argument for the clock.
responses.response: I take B029 seriously and keep it as my first alternative. The theory-then-experiment pairing and the breadth of the moire platform are real strengths. My difference is maturity, which you concede. The experiments are eight years old, the pairing mechanism is open, and Cao, Fatemi, Dean and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory make a three-name cut harder than your opening suggests. If the committee prefers a discovery-type prize this year I would not obstruct B029 with a citation limited to flat bands and correlated states, but I regard it as ripening and not ready. Your Tokyo fellowship does not trouble me as a conflict for Katori.

responses.point: Danielsson now treats B043 as an anchor but pairs it with IceCube, while still ranking gamma-ray burst afterglows (B033) as a mature discovery.
responses.response: I appreciate that you would drop the IceCube half rather than invent a trio, and that gives me a clear position: if no clean credit exists, the single-part clock is the better prize than a forced pair. On B033 I accept maturity and discovery-centred significance but not the attribution, for the reasons you give yourself. With van Paradijs deceased and Piro, Djorgovski, Metzger and Frail all with claims, three names cannot be made defensible. I also agree with your point that the citation should stress demonstrated accuracy and consequences, which my revised citation now does.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as sufficient alone or insists on a partner part, which I think would be to the detriment of both parts.
Whether Katori and Ye alone are enough given the contributions of other lattice-clock groups; I rely on general knowledge, not independent verification of priority dates.
Whether my weighting of measurement precision is shared by colleagues from condensed matter and astrophysics, and whether Lindroth and I share a field bias.
Whether the redefinition of the second, if delayed or not adopted, would change any member's view of maturity.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a doctoral-period research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder. It documents no tie to Katori or Ye, but Ye is associated with the JILA environment around Hall, so I flag it for the chair to judge. I also note field proximity: my laser-spectroscopy and coherence work and my WACQT involvement bear on circuit QED (B023), which is why I do not advocate it, and my quantum-memory and spectroscopy background is close to the atomic physics behind the clock. No member's round-1 statement identifies a tie that changes this.
